description: Interested in finding the next big discovery in our solar system? Explore observations by building a tool that uses image processing and pattern recognition to identify changes and flag potential moving object candidates. Such vast amounts of space data, who knows what discoveries might be hiding in plain sight? Perhaps we'll find something worth investigating as we search for the next Pluto! Interested in machine learning, data analysis, astronomy, image processing, or scientific visualization.
summary: Ulysses is built for NASA’s SPHEREx Science and Archive Team (Caltech/IPAC) so anyone can learn to spot cosmic motion while doing it—turning public curiosity into verifiable candidate triage across NASA’s $340M+ infrared sky survey. Each control keeps a plain sentence for what it just did, and a drill-down opens the rule underneath — why 102 channels become Hot and Cold, what a detector pixel is, and how two taps become a shift — so someone can finish one patch without a manual. Automated AI pipelines fail at SPHEREx’s thermal noise floor—lacking training data for unobserved targets like Planet X and flooding researchers with millions of false positives—while existing sky viewers hand people intimidating instrument dashboards. Ulysses queries live SPHEREx DR1 cutouts at 0.02°, 0.05°, or 0.15° through NASA IRSA’s public SIA service, keeps up to six visits, and encodes the coordinates, patch, mode, band, and marks inside a shareable URL. It folds the wavelengths into Hot (D1–D2) and Cold (D4–D6), one visit and one wavelength at a time, and subtracts the first visit from the current one so light means brighter now and dark means fainter. Users trace a knot across two dates with Pattern ID marks, read the shift in frame pixels, and save a snapshot of that frame on the device. The same link reopens the view for someone else to check, in under five minutes.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
**Our focus isn’t building another cluttered sky viewer for experts—it’s helping complete beginners learn how to spot real cosmic motion while doing it.
Ulysses is an open-standard data-triage tool built for NASA’s SPHEREx Science and Archive Team (Caltech/IPAC) that turns multi-epoch infrared sky surveys into a fast, verifiable motion-detection pipeline. In under five minutes, someone with zero astronomy background can inspect a patch of sky, isolate moving objects from static background noise, and log reproducible candidate coordinates.

Under the hood, Ulysses connects directly to NASA IRSA’s Simple Image Access (SIA) service to pull live SPHEREx DR1 cutouts (0.02°, 0.05°, or 0.15° fields of view) across up to six sequential visits. It groups SPHEREx’s 102 infrared channels (0.75–5.0 μm) into Hot (detectors D1–D2) and Cold (detectors D4–D6) regimes, lets users subtract baseline visits to reveal moving dipoles, and hides unusable pixels via native frame metadata flags. Tracing a source across dates calculates exact pixel displacement and encodes the entire analytical state into a shareable URL.

Benefits & Intended Impact NASA invested over $340 million into SPHEREx, producing a billion-object dataset that outpaces human scientific bandwidth. Automated AI pipelines fail at SPHEREx’s thermal noise floor—lacking training data for unobserved targets like Planet X and flooding researchers with millions of false positives from cosmic rays and crowded starfields. By compressing volunteer onboarding to five minutes, Ulysses offloads initial candidate triage from specialist desks, saving saved snapshots (coordinates, subtraction state, detector band, and trajectory marks) for peer review and candidate export.

Tools, Languages & Stack Built as a landscape-first web application using React, TypeScript, and HTML5 Canvas for frame-by-frame rendering, baseline subtraction, and trajectory overlays, styled with Material Design 3 tonal tokens and developed in Cursor.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

  • The difference is learnability: each control keeps a plain sentence for what it just did, and a drill-down opens the rule underneath — why 102 channels become Hot and Cold, what a detector pixel is, and how two taps become a shift — so a new person can finish one patch confidently, and understand everything about SphereX in just five minutes.
  • Turning Raw Noise into Intuitive Motion: Rather than burying users in 102 spectral channels and cryptic instrument settings, Ulysses folds SPHEREx data into plain-language thermal regimes (Hot vs. Cold) and baseline subtraction, rendering real grayscale archive counts untouched beneath clean Pattern ID vector trails.
  • Reproducible, Zero-Backend Triage: Every snapshot locks the exact sky coordinates, cutout scale, subtraction mode, and user trajectory marks directly into the URL and browser gallery—allowing anyone to reopen, audit, and validate a candidate view identically without custom server overhead
